content: Ceftazidime can reduce the effectiveness of oral hormonal contraceptives (levonorgestrel/ethinyl estradiol/ferrous bisglycinate) by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral forms of hormonal contraceptives. The risk of contraceptive failure is low, but caution and monitoring are advised. Antibiotics, in general, may decrease the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives. Ceftazidime can reduce the effectiveness of oral microbiota products containing bacterial spores through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Antibacterial agents may decrease the efficacy of these products if co-administered. It is recommended to complete antibiotic regimens 2–4 days before initiating oral microbiota therapy. Close monitoring is necessary. Ceftazidime increases the toxicity of neomycin (oral) due to nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Cephalosporins, including ceftazidime, may enhance the nephrotoxic effects of aminoglycosides. Close monitoring is required. Ceftazidime may reduce the effectiveness of immune checkpoint inhibitors such as nivolumab, pembrolizumab, penpulimab, sintilimab, tislelizumab, and toripalimab through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Co-administration may interfere with the therapeutic effects of these agents. Caution and close monitoring are advised. Ceftazidime increases the toxicity of plazomicin, streptomycin, and tobramycin due to nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Co-administration with drugs associated with nephrotoxicity may increase the risk of acute or chronic nephrotoxicity. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. Probenecid increases the levels or effects of ceftazidime by competing for renal tubular clearance. Caution and monitoring are advised. Ceftazidime may reduce the effectiveness of sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/anhydrous citric acid by altering colonic bacterial flora required for drug activation. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. Ceftazidime may reduce the effectiveness of live typhoid vaccine through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Live bacterial vaccines should not be administered until antibiotic therapy is completed. This interaction is contraindicated. Ceftazidime increases the effects of warfarin through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Caution and monitoring are advised. Ceftazidime may increase the levels or effects of acidic (anionic) drugs such as salicylates (non-ASA), sulfasalazine, and willow bark by competing for renal tubular clearance. The clinical significance of these interactions is unknown. Ceftazidime may cause transient increases in transaminases (3–9%), eosinophilia (<7%), diarrhea (<2%), immune hypersensitivity reactions (2%), phlebitis (<2%), rash (maculopapular or erythematous) (2%), thrombocytosis (2%), and injection site pain (1%). Other potential adverse effects include abdominal pain, agranulocytosis, angioedema, asterixis, coma, dizziness, encephalopathy, fever, hallucinations, increased serum bilirubin, leukopenia, lymphocytosis, metallic taste, myoclonia, nausea or vomiting, neuromuscular excitability, neutropenia, paresthesia, photosensitivity, pruritus, seizures, thrombocytopenia, transient increases in blood urea nitrogen (BUN) or serum creatinine, and urticaria. Patients with documented hypersensitivity to ceftazidime, cephalosporins, penicillins, or other beta-lactam antibiotics should not use this drug. High and prolonged serum ceftazidime concentrations can occur in patients with renal insufficiency, leading to seizures, nonconvulsive status epilepticus (NCSE), encephalopathy, coma, asterixis, neuromuscular excitability, and myoclonus. Dosage adjustments based on creatinine clearance are necessary in patients with renal impairment. Elevated international normalized ratio (INR) has been reported in patients with nutritional deficiencies, prolonged treatment, or renal or hepatic disease. Use with caution in patients with a history of seizure disorders, especially in renal impairment, where drug levels may significantly increase. Dose modification is required in renal impairment. Use with caution in patients with a history of penicillin allergy. Prescribing ceftazidime in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection or prophylactic indication is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. Ceftazidime is classified as Pregnancy Category B. It is excreted in breast milk; use with caution during lactation. Ceftazidime is a third-generation cephalosporin with broad-spectrum gram-negative activity, including Pseudomonas, but lower efficacy against gram-positive organisms. It inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins, thereby arresting bacterial growth. It is widely distributed in body tissues and fluids, including the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) when meninges are inflamed. It is not metabolized and is primarily excreted unchanged in the urine (80–90%). The half-life is 1–2 hours, and it is dialyzable by both hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis. Ceftazidime is compatible with certain drugs (e.g., amikacin, aminophylline, ciprofloxacin, gentamicin, ranitidine) but incompatible with others (e.g., amiodarone, amphotericin B, azithromycin, clarithromycin, vancomycin) depending on concentration. Store intact vials at room temperature, protected from light.
